title: Brain Structure
content_html:
Brain Structure

Division Description Primary Roles
Forebrain (Prosencephalon) Largest and most complex region; includes the cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, and limbic system. Conscious thought, memory, emotion, sensory processing, voluntary movement.
Midbrain (Mesencephalon) Connects forebrain to hindbrain; part of brainstem. Visual and auditory reflexes, motor control, arousal.
Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon) Includes pons, medulla oblongata, and cerebellum. Autonomic functions, balance, coordination, and sleep regulation.

Cerebrum and Cerebral Cortex

The cerebrum forms ~80% of brain mass and is divided into two hemispheres (left/right), connected by the corpus callosum. Each hemisphere contains four major lobes with distinct yet interconnected functions.

Lobe Location Key Functions
Frontal Front of brain Planning, decision-making, attention, voluntary motor control, working memory, social behaviour, language production (Broca’s area).
Parietal Upper middle Sensory integration, spatial reasoning, body awareness, numerical and symbolic processing.
Temporal Sides (near ears) Hearing, language comprehension (Wernicke’s area), long-term memory, emotion (limbic connections).
Occipital Back Vision — from simple edges to complex visual forms.

Within the cortex, grey matter (neuronal cell bodies) overlays white matter (myelinated axons). The cortex’s columnar architecture underlies the brain’s parallel distributed processing — analogous to nodes and edges in a computational network.

Limbic System (Emotion–Memory Hub)

A network of evolutionarily older structures beneath the cortex, the limbic system forms the core of Select – Change – Reconstruct in biological terms: emotion guides attention (Select), plasticity changes synaptic weights (Change), and recall reconstructs affective meaning (Reconstruct).

Structure Function
Hippocampus Encoding and retrieval of episodic memories; spatial navigation; consolidation during sleep (replay).
Amygdala Emotional tagging of memories; fear, salience, motivation; modulates hippocampal encoding.
Cingulate Cortex Emotional regulation; error detection; linking cognition and emotion.
Fornix / Mammillary Bodies Connect hippocampus to hypothalamus — part of declarative memory circuitry.
Nucleus Accumbens Reward learning, motivation, reinforcement (dopaminergic pathways).

Thalamus and Hypothalamus

Structure Role
Thalamus Central relay station: routes sensory signals to cortex; regulates attention and consciousness; key node in thalamo-cortical oscillations (brain rhythms).
Hypothalamus Maintains homeostasis (temperature, hunger, circadian rhythm); links nervous and endocrine systems; modulates emotion and motivation.

Basal Ganglia

The dopamine circuits here form the substrate of reinforcement learning — a biological analogue of computational feedback loops.

Structure Function
Caudate Nucleus, Putamen, Globus Pallidus, Substantia Nigra, Subthalamic Nucleus Action selection, habit formation, motor learning, procedural memory, and prediction of reward.

Cerebellum

Now understood as a predictive engine, the cerebellum creates internal models of movement and thought — learning through error correction. So in addition to motor coordination and balance, it is also predictive: timing and rhythm (temporal prediction) plus cognitive prediction and working memory (via prefrontal loops). The cerebellum embodies the “Change” phase — continual fine-tuning through feedback.

Brainstem

Region Function
Midbrain Reflexes, dopamine pathways (reward/motivation).
Pons Relay between cortex and cerebellum; regulates sleep and dreaming.
Medulla Oblongata Autonomic control (breathing, heart rate, reflexes).
Reticular Formation Arousal, wakefulness, attention — the “on/off” background of consciousness.

Neural Networks and Connectivity

  • Default Mode Network (DMN): Introspection, imagination, autobiographical memory.
  • Salience Network: Detects important stimuli; toggles between DMN and task networks.
  • Central Executive Network: Working memory, problem-solving, planning.
  • Hippocampal–Cortical Loops: Replay and consolidation during sleep and daydreaming.
  • Mirror Neuron System: Social learning, empathy, self–other mapping.

These dynamic networks exemplify parallel processing without a global clock — activity flows continuously through synchronised oscillations and recurrent feedback, not sequential programmatic steps.

Integrative Perspective — “Select – Change – Reconstruct”

Process Neural Basis Representative Structures
Select (Attention & Encoding) Competition for salience and focus Thalamus, sensory cortex, amygdala, prefrontal cortex
Change (Storage & Plasticity) Synaptic modification, replay, consolidation Hippocampus, cerebellum, basal ganglia
Reconstruct (Recall & Imagination) Pattern completion, integration with self-model Hippocampus–DMN loop, temporal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex
